comments.author: blagie
comments.text:
I am the author of multiple AGPL systems, many in mainstream use. Early LLM models would spit out my code almost verbatim. Modern systems borrow heavily on the creative design of those systems.
One company first pirated my AGPL code (e.g. shipped it without my name, copyright notices, source availability, etc.). I sent them violation notices. After many months of fighting, they had an LLM clone the system. The LLM clone feels:
a) Buggy and bad compared to my code
b) Still, like it's basically my creative content
It's as if you asked an LLM to rewrite Harry Potter, with the same plot, but bad dialogue.

comments.author: saikiran91
comments.text: I don’t know about one-shot-prompt toy apps, but when it comes to building real stuff with AI, it still takes significant effort from devs to get the results we need. There’s a difference, right? “Give me the best result” vs “Give me the result I want”. Most serious projects, at least from what I know, run on the “Give me the result I want” principle, and that’s where the dev effort goes. I know the future is heading toward “Give me the best result with no mistakes”, but that changes how much effort it takes, not who owns the output. Even if the code is generated by AI, humans own the result, because they worked with the machine to get the result they wanted. comments.author: viraptor
comments.text:
Doe v. GitHub already decided (I'm simplifying, read the actual thing yourself) that LLM output is not automatically open source - or specifically it doesn't infringe on the open source training material and doesn't inherit the oss copyright notice.
Thaler v. Perlmutter (again simplified) showed 100% AI output can't be given any copyright.
The directions the current cases are going are very much opposed to that idea and I wouldn't expect things to change in the opposite direction.

comments.author: glitchc
comments.text:
The article contradicts itself.
It's important to remember that the purpose of the license is to allow the copyright owner to exercise their rights in a manner they deem fit. Even if they choose to give the code away, that choice is captured in the form of a specifically worded license (MIT, BSD, etc.).
This means that licenses exist because code is copyrightable in the first place, with the license governing the use of said copyright. If AI code is not copyrightable, then no license can govern it.

Because to be clear, 90%+ of all code being written today is LLM-generated, so OP suggests that companies should no longer have any privacy wrt their internal software, all LLM code just gets yeeted into the public. possibly

“The PWM behavior is interesting, because we can see DC-dimming for all brightness levels. Usually, OLED panels use DC-Dimming only at higher brightness levels. The frequency is very low at 240 Hz, however, and this might be an issue for sensitive users, despite the DC-dimming. ”

comments.author: Velocifyer
comments.text:
I'm glad that this is bringing attention to flicker sensitivity.
Here are some other things that people are sensitive to:
- CRI on white LEDs (and flourencents).
CRI is how clean the spectrum is in comparison to the sun or a incandescent bulb, where the specturm is completely even. There are some CRI >=95 LEDs that are fine for most people however.
- Motion blur
Motion blur on LCDs (such as ~50% of Nintendo Switch 2s) can hurt eyes trying to keep track of what is going on.

comments.author: skocznymroczny
comments.text:
I had the same problem when the switch from CRT to LCD screens happened. I would get very dizzy when using them for a longer period of time. Other people looked at me funny. A lot of the LED bulbs are also flickering and can cause this issue. You can use the phone camera in pro mode to change the shutter speed to something like 1/8000 and it will show you the flickers.
Recently I switched from a 1440p IPS display which had no visible flickers on camera to OLED which has the flicker and the issues of headaches and dizziness came back. I can sometimes get used to it, but it's still straining more than the previous display did.

comments.author: explosion-s
comments.text:
As someone who’s had a concussion, this is really interesting. For me this is how any screen was to me, not just bright  OLED ones. Even more interestingly it’s essentially only screens— backlist posters at the mall (paper with a backlight) still affect it but less so. To me perhaps it’s focusing on something on a screen that does this, but it’s really interesting to see this affect the general population.
It’s also odd to think about lack of ability to concentrate, and I wonder if screens cause this optically somehow but to a less noticeable degree even when less intense than this new one? (Independent distracting contents)
I noticed that adding a severe red filter to all my screens helped me significantly with the concussion and am also curious about that, would that impact the intensity of a refresh perhaps? Is blue light specifically the problem? I’m unsure but have a plethora of subjective experience.
I’m glad for this to enter public consciousness a bit and would love to see more research on the screen itself impacting our brain.

comments.author: a-dub
comments.text:
macbook pro displays (before the oled) have always caused a weird sort of eyestrain and become hard to read after a few hours of usage for me. i have never pinned down exactly what causes it- some internet threads talk about "temporal dithering" complete with weird extensions that may or may not disable it. sometimes i wonder if it's the glossy display (although oddly sometimes it appears to affect me with external displays). i don't know if it's the glare from the gloss, the antialiasing of the fonts or something about the refresh? i have played with all the refresh rate "pro-motion" knobs, it doesn't seem to matter. many of my thinkpads have used pwm dimming, so it's not that. it has been an issue for me on both intel and aarch macbooks.
it would be interesting to get a high speed camera and see if there's a difference in the temporal dimension as well as a careful analysis of the font rendering. it would be funny if there were some kind of metamer noise in there or something that only some people have sensitivity to.
i would also be curious if the matte display option solves it (or has solved it for anyone else).

comments.text:
This article is only about understanding the implementation of positional embeddings, but to really understand positional embeddings you have to understand the theory. Positional embeddings are group representations. This is how you find them, and this is also how you parameterize them to make them differentiable/learnable. To give a few examples:
1. Rotary positional embeddings are representations of the translation group. The n-dimensional translation group ℝⁿ is abelian, so its irreducible representations are all one-dimensional ρ: ℝⁿ → ℂ, specified by a momentum vector m: ρₘ(x) = exp(i⟨m, x⟩). You can get a multi-dimensional representation by choosing several m, which are your learnable parameters.

The irreducible representations in four dimensions are your familiar particles: electrons, protons, etc., and in general are parameterized by a momentum vector and a discrete spin vector. stories.title_en: How did Woz write the Apple 1 BASIC before building the computer?

comments.author: femto
comments.text:
What Woz did was the default way of writing assembly language programs for owners of 8-bit computers (mostly hobbyists).  You didn't have money for a second machine, so you wrote your program on paper, you entered it then tested it in situ.  Mostly you got it right, as doing it on paper was slow and meant you had the opportunity to put lots of thought into it.  8-bit instruction sets were simple enough that you eventually learned the most common instructions by heart.  There was a point where I could mostly translate a Z80 program from assembly to machine code from (my) memory.
Maybe that is part of the nostalgia for the 8-bit days: the practice of "slow programming"?  It was relaxing, sort of like those "slow tv" shows.

comments.author: kamma4434
comments.text:
For what it’s worth: when I used to do assembly on the commodore 64, after a while, your eyes are so used to seeing A9 close to LDA let you start knowing them by heart without even thinking. Of course this is possible on 6502 and will be way harder on modern CPUs. In the end of the number of common opcodes might have been 30-50, and you can always look up the rest from a one-page table.
I remember that was a book that went on to say that you should learn machine code (that is, raw opcodes), not assembly, to program the c-64. Not sure I would agree, but it’s definitely feasible.
The only thing that is strange in the Woz story is that you would usually start by creating a dirt-poor monitor/assembler so that you would have a sane environment to do further development in. That was the approach manuals from the era suggested for new hardware (eg Rodnay Zack’s)

It was also pretty common to use BASIC to POKE in a quick bootstrap program to load a value in a register and jump to an address, which I could usually do from memory. comments.author: igorandri
comments.text:
Igor here, Head of Security at Lovable. Thanks to the Crissy Field team for their work.
The root cause in these apps was insufficent Row-Level Security, which is exactly what our scanning is built to catch. We scan every app automatically before publish and offer a deeper SAST scan, both free for all users. When we flag findings, users can select “Fix” and Lovable will help resolve them. They can also enable auto-fix, which resolves security findings in the background, and block publishing entirely when there are critical findings.
When an app has end users, security is a key part of the product. That’s why we keep investing in making security tools better and easier to use, taking on as much of the security load as we can and fixing more issues automatically.
I personally believe that making security accessible is what leads to making software accessible. We’re committed to both.
You can read more about our approach:
https://lovable.dev/blog/find-it-fix-it-ship-it
